title: When a Group Makes Cooperation Pay — Hobbes & Ostrom Self-Governance, Fehr & Gächter (2000) Costly Peer Punishment & Gächter, Renner & Sefton’s (2008) 10-Round vs. 50-Round Net-Earnings Reversal in Public-Goods Games

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: In short 10-round lab games, letting players pay $1 to fine free-riders $3 rescues contributions—yet initially burns up group profits in punishment crossfire! Stretch the same group to 50 rounds (Gachter, Renner & Sefton 2008), and credible deterrence makes cooperation genuinely pay off.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Human institutions—from village commons to religious norms—depend on time horizons: costly enforcement looks wasteful in brief encounters unless relationships last long enough for norms to stabilize.
keyTakeaways: Without sanctions, public-goods contributions steadily unravel toward free-riding even when everyone would be richer cooperating.
Fehr & Gachter (2000) showed costly peer punishment sustains high contributions, and Shariff & Norenzayan (2007) explored implicit supernatural-monitoring primes in anonymous dictator games.

Gachter, Renner & Sefton (2008) solved a major puzzle: in 10 rounds, punishment destruction often lowers net group earnings below no-punishment games, whereas across 50 partner rounds punishment drops near zero once cooperation locks in—yielding big net welfare gains.

vocab.meaning: Experimental dilemma where individual tokens contributed to a group pot multiply for everyone, tempting selfish free-riding.
Spending personal payoff to reduce a norm violator's payoff, even when the punisher pays an immediate cost.
How longer repeated interaction horizons transform costly enforcement into cheap deterrence.

quiz.question: What flipped net group earnings from negative/flat to strongly positive in Gachter, Renner & Sefton's (2008) Science experiment?
options: Extending repeated partner interactions from 10 rounds to 50 rounds so initial punishment established stable cooperation with minimal ongoing fines
quiz.explanation: Over 50 rounds, contributions stayed near 90% while actual punishment expenditures fell sharply after early rounds, making net earnings far exceed non-punishment groups.
